structure.title: Part I · Waiting for a boat
structure.text: A man on a yacht in the Thames remembers his first command in Africa. Before he can sail upriver, Marlow encounters a European office, a chain gang and a damaged steamer. The company ostensibly devoted to efficient trade seems incapable of delivering the rivets he needs.

structure.title: Part II · Reports travel downstream
structure.text: Kurtz reaches Marlow as an impressive quantity of ivory, an artist, a rival and a remarkable voice. Upstream progress requires an attention to snags, shoals and fog quite different from the Europeans' preoccupation with the man at the far station.

structure.title: Part III · Who may speak for Kurtz
structure.text: The journey brings Marlow close enough to compare the talk with material evidence of what happened at the station. Later, people who knew Kurtz elsewhere lay claim to different versions of him. Deciding what to tell becomes part of what Marlow brings home.

people.name: Marlow
people.text: He has done the work he describes and remembers the physical satisfaction of doing it well. His listeners can hear him hesitate over how to describe people he scarcely knew. The story preserves his limitations along with his testimony.

people.name: Kurtz
people.text: Kurtz has enough admirers and enemies to seem familiar before he appears. Almost everyone praising his gifts has a stake in his reputation. The people among whom his station operates have far fewer opportunities to say what his success cost them.

context.title: Hearing Africa through a European narrator
context.text: The book shows forced labour and lethal exploitation while giving European agents far more speech and individual history than the Africans they encounter. Even a description that condemns cruelty can leave the victim almost entirely outside its account of human experience.

context.title: Ivory determines the promotions
context.text: The company measures a station’s performance in tusks sent downriver. A successful agent may be rewarded despite the methods he uses to meet that target. Marlow therefore has to ask what sort of distinction he is hearing about whenever another official praises Kurtz’s results.

notice.text: Compare names with the objects they cover.
notice.why: Words about progress, trade and duty circulate freely around broken machinery and starving labourers. The broken equipment is often described in sharper individual detail than the people meant to operate it.

notice.text: Listen for the river behind the storyteller.
notice.why: A listener occasionally remembers the yacht and the darkening Thames. The European capital whose ships set out to govern distant places is still there whenever Marlow pauses to take a breath.

opening: Marlow takes a job piloting a steamer into the Congo, where a European trading company speaks of civilisation and measures success in ivory. The farther he travels, the harder those two descriptions become to reconcile. Everyone talks about Kurtz, an exceptional agent whose results seem to excuse almost anything. Conrad builds the journey out of delays, rumours, and glimpses of violence, making the desire to meet this remarkable man entangle the reader in the same fascination that has helped protect him from scrutiny.
